research_page.title: Remternetug in early Alzheimer's (TRAILRUNNER-ALZ 3)
research_page.description: A Phase 3 trial registry protocol evaluating the subcutaneous anti-amyloid immunotherapy remternetug for delaying clinical progression in early Alzheimer's disease.
research_page.takeaway_md: TRAILRUNNER-ALZ 3 is a large, multi-year Phase 3 trial testing whether subcutaneous remternetug can delay clinical progression in early Alzheimer's disease. With a primary completion timeline extending to 2030, it aims to establish long-term efficacy and safety for this next-generation administration route.
key_findings_md: The trial targets individuals aged 55-80 with biomarker-confirmed amyloid pathology but minimal to no current cognitive impairment (source: Eligibility).
The primary endpoint evaluates the time to clinically meaningful progression on the Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) scale over up to 255 weeks (source: Primary outcome measures).
Participants are randomized to receive either subcutaneous remternetug or a placebo (source: Arms and Interventions).
research_page.methods_md: This is a Phase 3, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial enrolling an estimated 1,400 adults aged 55 to 80. Participants must have P-tau levels consistent with amyloid pathology but minimal cognitive and functional impairment. The study spans up to 255 weeks to evaluate time to clinical progression.
research_page.trial_evidence_md: This trial evaluates the long-term clinical efficacy of remternetug, following the earlier [TRAILRUNNER-ALZ 1](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05463731) trial, which focused on amyloid clearance and self-administration feasibility. It serves as a pivotal study to confirm whether subcutaneous delivery provides sustained disease modification and delays cognitive decline.
research_page.sentiment_md: Public sentiment is highly optimistic, driven by patient and caregiver hopes that a subcutaneous injection will eliminate the burden of IV infusions and enable simple at-home treatment. Retail investors also view this delivery method as a competitive advantage for Eli Lilly. However, mainstream biotech media remains cautious, pointing to high ARIA (brain swelling) rates in earlier anti-amyloid data that complicate the vision of unmonitored at-home use.
caveats_md: This document outlines study design and protocols for a trial that recently began; it does not contain clinical results.
Despite public hopes for near-term availability, this specific Phase 3 trial is not scheduled to complete until October 2030.
Enthusiasm for casual at-home administration may outpace reality if the drug requires rigorous MRI monitoring for ARIA, similar to other anti-amyloid therapies.
relates_to_md: [Amyloid hypothesis](/research/amyloid-hypothesis) — The underlying biological mechanism being targeted.

trial_pages.title: TRAILRUNNER-ALZ 3
trial_pages.description: Phase 3 trial evaluating subcutaneous remternetug versus placebo in early Alzheimer's disease.
trial_pages.population: Adults aged 55-80 with P-tau consistency for amyloid and minimal cognitive impairment (n=1400)
trial_pages.primary_endpoint: Time to Clinically Meaningful Progression as Measured by Clinical Dementia Rate Scale (CDR)
trial_pages.why_md: This trial seeks to determine if subcutaneous administration of remternetug can delay cognitive and functional decline over a prolonged period (up to 255 weeks). It addresses the need for less burdensome administration routes in anti-amyloid therapy while measuring long-term disease modification.

timeline_entries.title: 2024-10 — TRAILRUNNER-ALZ 3 trial begins
timeline_entries.body_md: Eli Lilly launches a Phase 3 trial evaluating subcutaneous remternetug in 1,400 participants with early Alzheimer's disease to measure time to clinical progression over 255 weeks. [Read more](/research/papers/remternetug-trailrunner-alz-3)

notes_for_editor: The sentiment researcher cited an ARIA rate of up to 41% from 'early data.' This is not present in the NCT06653153 registry document. I retained references to ARIA in the sentiment and caveats sections as a general known risk of anti-amyloids to contextualize the hype around 'at-home administration,' but the specific 41% figure requires external verification.
